A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Value Improved Actor Critic Algorithms and retain the identifiable two-operator framework. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices support comparison, including v1 Appendices A–C and v2 Appendices A–D.

before.justification: v1 reports original MuJoCo experiments evaluating VI-DDPG and VI-TD3, including baseline comparisons and ablations in Section 6 and Appendix B.

after.justification: v2 reports original DeepMind Control experiments evaluating VI-TD3, VI-SAC, and VI-TD7, plus greedification and computational-budget analyses in Section 4 and Appendix A.

M1.justification: The two-operator framework remains, but v1's mean-top-k and two-stage Gaussian sampling designs for VI-DDPG/TD3 give way to expectile-loss variants of TD3, SAC, and TD7. v2 also introduces repeated-gradient improvement of a copied target policy and a simpler sampling variant, with explicit and implicit VI-AC algorithms in Appendix B.

E1.justification: The six Gym MuJoCo tasks in v1 are replaced by twelve DeepMind Control tasks in v2. Coverage now includes distinct standing, hopping, walking, and running objectives, plus fish-swim, acrobot-swingup, and quadruped tasks. This changes represented environments and task requirements, rather than merely renaming benchmarks.

E2.justification: TD3 remains a comparator, while the evaluated DDPG, PPO, and MPO comparisons in v1 disappear. v2 evaluates SAC and TD7 against their value-improved variants in Figures 1 and 5, and adds TD3 comparisons with increased acting-policy updates and replay ratios.

E3.justification: Main benchmark budgets change from task-dependent 1, 3, or 10 million steps to 3 million steps per DeepMind Control task. New protocols measure bootstrap improvement and value-estimation bias and control gradient-update budgets. The reported TD3 output activations also change from tanh critic/linear actor to linear critic/tanh actor; the PDFs do not establish whether this corrects documentation or implementation.

E4.justification: v1's double-critic ablations and sampling-hyperparameter sweeps are replaced by analyses of expectile strength, repeated value-policy gradient steps, bootstrap gaps, estimation bias, acting-policy updates, and replay ratios. v2 Appendix A.2 additionally compares implicit, gradient-based, and sampling-based improvement, substantially revising the mechanisms and tradeoffs investigated.

E5.justification: Both versions retain the main 20-seed/two-standard-error and ablation 10-seed/one-standard-error conventions. However, v1 Appendix B Figure 4 additionally displays standard-deviation bands for the main experiments; v2 omits this supplementary view of variability.

E6.justification: The MuJoCo return curves and DDPG double-critic findings are replaced by DeepMind Control results for VI-TD3, VI-SAC, and VI-TD7. New findings include expectile VI-TD3 leading the sampling and gradient variants on both hopper tasks in Figure 6, and degradation with excessive expectile greedification in Figure 3. These are results under different methods and settings, not same-setting version-to-version gains.

T1.justification: v2 retains the earlier backward-induction convergence argument in Appendices C.9–C.11 but substantially expands the theory. It adds necessary and bounded greedification conditions, counterexamples, finite-step convergence arguments, Gumbel MuZero operator lemmas and a convergence corollary, and relaxes the second operator's requirement to non-detrimental improvement.

C1.justification: The core value-improvement proposal remains, but v2 adds contribution claims about necessary conditions, two sufficient operator classes, and convergence underlying Gumbel MuZero. Its abstract and conclusion replace the VI-DDPG/TD3 MuJoCo claim with VI-TD3/SAC results in DeepMind Control and a negligible-cost implementation claim, emphasizing control of the greedification–stability tradeoff.

C2.justification: v1 emphasizes sampling robustness and dependence on double critics to mitigate overestimation. v2 interprets its new controls as evidence for benefits from evaluated-policy greedification and reduced interaction with acting-policy instability. Appendix D.3 adds the substantive limitation that direct expectile regression can become risk-seeking in stochastic environments, explaining the deterministic-environment implementation choice.

D1.justification: v2 Appendix D documents target-policy copying and gradient updates, 128-action sampling, direct expectile regression, SAC/TD7 implementation sources and hyperparameters, and TD7's non-prioritized replay buffer. Conversely, v1 Appendix C.6's detailed GPU, CPU, RAM, and wall-clock accounting is removed, although v2 acknowledges the computing facilities.

R1.justification: v2 adds substantial engagement with Gumbel MuZero, implicit Q-learning, greedification-operator research, REDQ, and TD7, while removing much of v1's survey of actor-critic convergence and policy/value equivalences. Section 5 also revises the positioning relative to MuZero Reanalyze and GreedyAC around whether acting and evaluated policies coincide.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, background, and related work are extensively rewritten around greedification and stability. Separate dynamic-programming sections are consolidated, practical methods and experiments are integrated into Section 4, and proofs, additional results, and pseudocode are reorganized across the appendices.

P2.justification: The figure suite is substantially redesigned: six-task benchmark panels become twelve-task grids, and new diagnostic columns and paired-task comparisons appear. Practical algorithm blocks are reworked in Appendix B, while the hyperparameter table changes from four algorithm groups to three with a revised grid and additional rows.

improvement.justification: v2's expectile implementation and targeted controls strengthen the practical and mechanistic evidence beyond v1's sampling-focused study. However, the new Gumbel MuZero proof in Appendix C.5, around Equations 28–30, incorrectly infers convergence of a sum from its terms approaching zero, leaving a prominent added convergence claim unproved as written. These empirical benefits and the substantive proof gap prevent a confident judgment of net overall improvement.
